title: Primary Congenital Glaucoma: The Buphthalmos Blueprint
summary: Primary Congenital Glaucoma (PCG) is a sight-threatening condition caused by isolated maldevelopment of the trabecular meshwork (trabeculodysgenesis). This comprehensive guide covers the pathognomonic clinical signs, essential Examination Under Anesthesia (EUA) protocols, and gold-standard surgical interventions required for vision preservation.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Primary Congenital Glaucoma (PCG) is defined as a form of developmental glaucoma characterized by an isolated developmental defect of the trabecular meshwork and anterior chamber angle (trabeculodysgenesis) that is not associated with other ocular or systemic anomalies. It results in obstructed aqueous outflow and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), leading to characteristic ocular stretching (buphthalmos) in the elastic infant eye.

rows: Flat or concave iris insertion; most common type.
Anterior iris stromal hypoplasia or structural iris defects.
Associations with Axenfeld-Rieger or Peters Anomaly (Secondary).

sections.title: The Pathognomonic Triad
content: 1. Epiphora (Excessive tearing)
2. Photophobia (Light sensitivity)
3. Blepharospasm (Involuntary eyelid squeezing)

sections.title: Clinical Signs & Ocular Exam
content: Buphthalmos: Corneal diameter >12mm in the first year.
Haab Striae: Horizontal or concentric ruptures in Descemet's membrane.
Corneal Edema: Ground-glass appearance from high IOP.
Optic Disc Cupping: Rapidly progressive but uniquely reversible if IOP is lowered.
Axial Length: Significant elongation measured by A-scan.

sections.title: EUA Protocol: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Immediate IOP measurement (Perkins or Tonopen) upon induction; avoid Halothane/Sevoflurane if possible as they lower IOP (Ketamine raises it).
Step 2: Measurement of Horizontal Corneal Diameter (White-to-White) using calipers.
Step 3: Gonioscopy using a Koeppe or Swan-Jacob lens to identify iris insertion level.
Step 4: Pachymetry to assess corneal thickness and edema state.
Step 5: Dilated Fundoscopy to assess C:D ratio and exclude retinal pathology.
Step 6: A-scan Ultrasonography for axial length measurement (tracking progression).

sections.title: Management & Surgical Algorithm
content: 1. Medical Temporization: Topical BB (caution with asthma) or CAI (Diamox 10-15 mg/kg/day).
2. Clear Cornea present? -> Perform Goniotomy (internal approach, 120-180 degrees).
3. Cloudy Cornea present? -> Perform Trabeculotomy (external approach with Harms trabeculotome).
4. Failure of Primary Surgery? -> Repeat Angle Surgery or 360-degree Trabeculotomy (illuminated microcatheter).
5. Refractory Cases? -> Mitomycin-C Trabeculectomy or Glaucoma Drainage Device (Ahmed/Baerveldt).
6. Last Resort? -> Diode Laser Cyclophotocoagulation.

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergency Signs
content: Sudden increase in corneal clouding (Acute Hydrops)
Rapidly increasing C:D ratio in an infant
Asymmetric corneal diameters (even 0.5mm)
Systemic BB side effects (Bradycardia, Apnea)
Loss of red reflex due to corneal opacity

content.explanation: DDx for Cloudy Cornea: Sclerocornea, Trauma, Ulcer, Metabolic (Mucopolysaccharidosis), Peters Anomaly, Edema (PCG), Dystrophy (CHED).

sections.title: Surgical Key Points
content: Goniotomy: Requires 100% visualization through a clear cornea.
Trabeculotomy: Gold standard when cornea is too cloudy to see angle.
Microcatheter-assisted 360-degree Trabeculotomy: Shows higher success rates than traditional methods.
Post-op Care: Prophylactic antibiotics and corticosteroids for 4 weeks.

sections.title: Complications & Long-term Prognosis
content: Amblyopia: Most common cause of vision loss (refractive/anisometropic).
High Myopia: Due to permanent axial elongation.
Lens Subluxation: In extreme cases of buphthalmos.
Lifelong Monitoring: 50% of successfully treated patients may require further surgery later in life.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Evidence
sections.content: Recent studies focus on 360-degree trabeculotomy using the iTrack microcatheter, which has demonstrated superior IOP lowering compared to standard 120-degree procedures. The BIG (British Infantile Glaucoma) study highlights that primary surgical intervention is significantly more effective than primary medical management. Genetic screening for CYP1B1 is now recommended for siblings in consanguineous families.
